extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history/Reformation-era biography; general readers of scholarly biography
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and methodological principles for composing and evaluating a scholarly biography (here: Erasmus) with emphasis on source-criticism, selection of materials, scope-limitation, and interpretation of actions versus words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological method
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have chosen the chronological method because it serves best to illustrate the development of the man in his relation to his time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a chronological framework to show development of subject in relation to historical context; this method helps trace changing attitudes and actions over time rather than treating life thematically or anachronistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select writings bearing on main objects
rubrics_metrics.description: "Such selections from Erasmus' writings have been chosen for detailed examination as bear most directly upon the main objects of the book."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose primary texts that directly illuminate the book's central questions; prefer representative, substantive passages rather than many disconnected scraps that can be contradictory or misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer longer passages to mere scraps
rubrics_metrics.description: "It has seemed wiser to make them long enough to show their true meaning rather than to use a greater number of mere scraps, which might in almost every case be contradicted by other scraps."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When quoting or analyzing, include sufficient context/length to capture the author's full meaning and avoid false contrasts produced by isolated excerpts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope according to series/purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "The limitations of the present volume have fortunately been clearly defined by the title of the series... Its function is to deal with Erasmus as a factor in the Protestant Reformation..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and adhere to a clear functional scope for the work (e.g., focus on subject as factor in a particular movement); only bring in biographical material that serves that defined purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid merely controversial detail
rubrics_metrics.description: "So far as possible the merely controversial has been avoided. For example, I have barely alluded to the prolonged discussions with Archbishop Lee... The detail of these controversies tends rather to confuse than to illuminate the point of chief interest to us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude or minimize protracted, arcane controversies that do not advance the central interpretive aim, since they can distract and confuse readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation fidelity with stylistic freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: "The translations have been kept as close to the originals as was consistent with a freedom of style somewhat corresponding to Erasmus' own."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate primary texts closely but allow for stylistic choices that preserve the character and liveliness of the original author; do not over-paraphrase to the point of losing voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourfold test of the subject's statements
rubrics_metrics.description: "At every stage of the study of Erasmus one has to ask first what he believed himself to be doing, then what he wished others to believe he was doing, then what others did think he was doing, and finally what the man actually was doing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each statement or document, interrogate (1) the subject's self-conception, (2) intended public impression, (3) contemporaries' perception, and (4) the factual record of actions; use this multi-angle test to evaluate reliability and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read letters with reference to their immediate purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: "The letters must therefore be read with constant reference to their immediate purpose, and few of them are without purpose..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat correspondence as purposeful communications (often edited, altered, or rhetorical). Analyze letters in light of audience, occasion, editorial revision, and possible self-fashioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for editorial revision and unreliability of published letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus 'revised the collection. Some things I explained... Some... I struck out. Some things I softened.' Also: the chronology is hopelessly confused; many letters were altered for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of published corpora compiled by the author: investigate provenance, revisions, dating, and editorial interventions; prefer critical editions and corroborating documentary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test words by actions (behavioural test)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only reasonable test is to be found in what he actually did."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims (e.g., professed loyalties, intentions, or attitudes), give decisive weight to documented conduct and choices rather than rhetorical statements alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix the line between history and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: "This essentially literary quality must be constantly borne in mind by the historian and he must always be striving to fix the line where history ends and literature begins."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate rhetorical/ literary devices and borrowed classical motifs from factual reportage; recognize when an author is literaryizing episodes and avoid treating such passages as straightforward history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of classical borrowing and formulaic reuse
rubrics_metrics.description: "Another source of confusion is Erasmus' amazing command of classic literature and his cleverness in utilising, not merely the forms, but at times the ideas and even the phrases of ancient authors.... He must be literary; he might be accurate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate classical echoes, allusions, and formulaic reuse to determine originality versus imitation; do not assume phrasing equals fact—classical rhetoric may shape descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat personal element cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where no such issue can be raised, as, for example, in the purely philological essays... we are often forced to admire the vigour and decision of Erasmus' utterance. But if his personal judgment was assailed... his sensitive temper was readily roused..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept works at face value where impersonal/technical; where personal stakes exist, allow for defensiveness, exaggeration, or strategic rhetoric—adjust credibility accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use critical scholarship and evaluate editions
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have used constantly the Leyden edition of Erasmus' works... The editorial work is meagre and careless... The indexes are... useless... the editor... leaves them as he finds them, and the reader is compelled to discover the inaccuracies for himself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the reliability of editions and secondary literature; consult recent critical studies and archival discoveries (e.g., Horawitz, Vischer, Fruin) and prefer scholarly, critical editions over older careless printings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about uncertain facts and avoid over-interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: "The singular thing is that with this great mass of material we know so little that is definite about him... The only safe method is, therefore, to try in each case to weigh the value of the text before us with fullest reference to all the circumstances."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where documentary evidence is confused or contradictory (dates of birth, familial claims, chronology), avoid definitive statements; present probabilities and the basis for uncertainty; weigh texts against full circumstantial evidence.
